extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in algebraic transformations, numerical solution of equations, and classical analytic methods
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked examples of Horner's algebraic-transformation procedures for manipulating polynomial coefficients, computing finite differences, and isolating/estimating polynomial roots; also several related classical results (parabola axes, special functions, geometry problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved transformation requiring half space/multiplicand figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The addends, after the first course, may be derived each from the nearest addends above and on the left hand of it, instead of from the sum beneath the latter; and by a mental process when 7 is a digit: a method which requires only half the space, and half the number of multiplicand figures which are employed in that of the preceding article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: multiply the equation by 7 and make Bm·7 = mB so that mB = m—1B + mA·7; then derive subsequent addends from neighbouring above/left addends rather than below sums. The author notes this process is more compact (half space and multiplicand figures) and attributes its non-appreciation to mathematicians, though it is deducible from earlier general theorems (arts. 13–18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for obtaining suite of finite differences (increment 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: When r = 1, the sum of all the addends to any term of the given formula is equal to the difference of that term; the first course of addends are the successive sums of the given coefficients, omitting the last; each following course consists of successive sums of the preceding course, stopping short of the last term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical model and example: form successive courses where each course is successive sums of the previous (one dimension lower when taking differences of differences). The work terminates at the 2^n course when dimensions are exhausted. This furnishes an 'easiest and most elegant method' of obtaining the suite of differences for every coefficient when increment is 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of successive transformées to locate limits of positive roots
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute terms of these transformations are equal to the results of substituting 0, 1, 2, ... for a in the given equation; the changes of signs which they exhibit between successive transformations indicate where roots begin (e.g., sign change between 4th and 5th transformées shows a root begins with 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: compute transformées (successive transformations of coefficients); read off absolute terms as polynomial evaluated at integers; sign changes between transformées show integer bounds for positive roots. Example given for 2°—632+189=0 demonstrates reading off beginnings of roots from sign changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplier-selection rule in the transformation tables
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplier for each term is invariably the smaller of the two exponents (that of the power to which it belongs and that of the transformée in which it stands). Consequently, in the 2nd and following transformations the multipliers are constantly 2, m—1, m—2, ... down to 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practice, indices and exponents may be numbered and indicated (e.g., m² directs to multiply p times by m, after which the multiplier is continually diminished by 1). Examples show how to apply varying marginal exponents and indicate abrupt changes as mp, m−a, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure-transformée variation (keeps indications constant)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variation adhering to pure transformées keeps every requisite indication constantly in view but lacks the neatness and rapidity of the direct method in ordinary cases, particularly when applied to high powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'general formule' builds each course of coefficients from successive sums of the preceding course (stopping short of the final term except at first summation); the new transformée is given and the entire process is a series of similar transformations. Use where keeping transformées explicit is advantageous despite slower computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine Horner transforms with Budan and De Gua criteria for initial solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Either of the described transformation processes, when combined with the discriminative use of Budan's criterion of impossible roots and De Gua's criterion, forms a very complete instrument of initial solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author recommends combining transformée-based coefficient analysis with Budan's rule (to detect impossibilities) and De Gua's tests (as exemplified in the author's prior paper) to form a robust procedure for initial localization and elimination of candidate root intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola criterion for general conic (B^2 − 4AC = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the general second-degree equation Ay^2 + Bxy + Cx^2 + Dy + Ex + F = 0, for the locus to be a parabola it must satisfy B^2 − 4AC = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author substitutes parametric expressions for coordinates of contact points with the tangent-axes and deduces A, B, C, D, E in terms of parameters; imposing B^2−4AC = 0 and reducing yields the specialized form (equation (6)) which must be examined under both signs, leading to straight-line factorization in one sign and the parabola equation in the other. The condition is given explicitly and used to derive the parabola referred to two tangents as axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derived equation forms when axes are two tangents (cases of signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the conic is referred to two tangents as axes and the discriminant vanishes, substituting the parameter values yields a bi-sign equation which for the positive sign reduces to a straight-line equation {(ay + bx) − ab}^2 = 0 and for the negative sign yields after manipulation the parabola equation (expressed in the text as ay + bx − ab = ±2√(abxy) leading to ay + bx = ab in transformed variables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author treats both sign-cases of the squared form and shows the positive sign gives a degenerate case (straight line) while the negative sign produces the proper parabola form; students are referred to further treatment for special case a=b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and limiting-product formulas for I(a+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Through manipulations of series Sm = 1^−m + 2^−m + 3^−m + ... and known product/trigonometric identities, expressions for I(a+1) are obtained as limits of finite products and infinite products; e.g., r(a+1)=limit of expressions involving products (1+ a/(...))(1+ ...), with trigonometric-product relationships given (equations (13)–(20) in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author appeals to De Morgan and other classical sources, forms limits of products P_n and relates log and trig expressions to derive formulae for I(a+1) and related identities (including substitutions and manipulations such as a→3a). Several intermediary logarithmic and trigonometric series expansions and limit arguments are used; the presentation emphasizes passing to limits of finite-product expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric theorems used as constructive criteria in circle problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Various constructive properties are stated and used as criteria: e.g., when a circle's circumference is divided into n equal parts and certain chords joined, the intersections OB_k give successive fractional parts of the radius (OB_n equals radius/(n+1)); tangents from an external point P, their midpoints, and perpendicular bisectors of chords through P concur; the tangents at chord intersections and the chord of contact intersect at a common point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are given as solved exercises (VIII, IX) with multiple synthetic and analytic solutions: use rhombus/parallel/similarity arguments for chord divisions; use coordinate geometry and midpoint/perpendicular constructions for tangent-midpoint concurrence; the results provide constructive checks and coordinate formulae for intersection points (co-ordinates provided in analytic solution).
